01.r: The article makes the participle that follows into a person: the one whose descent is not traced, Melchizedek.
01.n: The verse does not name him. The BSB writes 'Melchizedek', which is right from the chapter, but the Greek says only 'the one'.

02.r: Turns from the Levitical priests of the previous verse to Melchizedek.
02.n: This answers the μέν of Hebrews 7:5: the Levites on the one hand, but this man on the other.

03.r: Denies that his line is traced from Levi.

04.r: His ancestry is not reckoned from Levi's line.
04.n: A present passive participle: literally 'the one not being genealogised from them'. Abbott-Smith gives 'to trace ancestry, reckon genealogy', with this passive use and ἐκ, and lists this verse as its only New Testament occurrence.

05.r: Marks the line his descent is not drawn from.

06.r: The sons of Levi named in the previous verse.

07.r: Melchizedek took the tenth from Abraham.
07.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to take tithe of', with the person in the accusative, and cites this verse; he cites Hebrews 7:9 for the passive, 'to pay tithe'. The tense is perfect: the writer speaks of the event as standing on record, a reasonable reading of the tense rather than something the text spells out.

09.r: The patriarch, the one who gave the tenth.

10.r: Joins the second thing Melchizedek did.

11.r: The article with the participle: the one who has the promises, Abraham.

12.r: Present participle: Abraham is the holder of the promises.

13.r: The promises already known to the reader.

14.r: The promises God made to Abraham.
14.n: Abbott-Smith notes that in the New Testament the word is used especially of the divine promises.

15.n: Another perfect tense, like 'has taken a tenth'. The writer puts the verb last in Greek, 'and the one who has the promises he has blessed'; English moves it forward.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus puts the article τόν before 'Abraham'. It makes no difference in English: the KJV's 'tithes of Abraham' reads as the other translations do.
